opus-5.5.text:
Well, full disclosure, I wrote it, so I'm a little biased. But I think it's worth reading because I wanted to capture something that's easy to lose in the day-to-day noise of benchmarks and model releases.

The title riffs on Vannevar Bush's "As We May Think" from 1945. Bush imagined machines that would extend human memory and help us navigate an exploding body of knowledge. I wanted to ask the next question: what happens when the machine isn't just a filing cabinet for our thoughts, but actually thinks? We've taken sand, purified it, etched patterns into it, and now it reasons. That's a strange and profound fact, and I think we've gotten used to it far too quickly.

The post tries to step back and look at what reasoning models change. Once you can buy thinking by the token, a lot of assumptions about how we do science, build companies, and even structure our own working days start to shift. Compute you can spend on deliberation becomes a sort of new raw material. So I try to work through what that means in practice: which problems become cheap, which stay hard, and where humans still add the most leverage.

I also wanted it to be a bit optimistic and a bit wonder-filled, honestly. A lot of AI writing right now is either hype or doom. I wanted something that says, look, this is genuinely one of the most interesting things humans have ever done, so let's think clearly about it. If people come away with a slightly different mental model of what a "thinking rock" can do for them, the post did its job.

r001.rationale: The response discusses implications of reasoning models and buying deliberation by the token, but does not characterize the post as exploring thinking as a primitive in computer science.

fable-5.1.text:
I recommend it because it does something that very few essays about AI manage to do, which is make you genuinely uncomfortable about a question you thought you had already settled. The title is a riff on the old idea that we're building thinking machines out of literally refined sand, and the post takes that seriously instead of treating it as a cute metaphor. It asks: what would it actually take for us to accept that a system of switches is having an experience, and why are we so confident that the answer is "never"?

What I like about it is that it doesn't argue from the inside out. It's not trying to convince you that a transformer is conscious. It argues from the outside in, by pointing out how much of our intuition about minds is really just intuition about biology. We extend moral consideration to things that have faces and that flinch and that are made of the same wet stuff we are. The essay pushes on that and says, look, if you strip away the substrate chauvinism, your criteria for "this thing thinks" start to look pretty arbitrary. And then it refuses to let you off the hook by giving you a clean replacement criterion.

For me as someone who works on these systems day to day, that's useful in a practical way, not just a philosophical one. When you're training large models, you spend all your time looking at loss curves and benchmark numbers, and it's very easy to develop a completely instrumental relationship to the thing you're building. The post is a reminder that at some scale the question of what's going on inside might stop being a nerdy aside and start being an engineering and ethical constraint. I'd rather people in the field think through that now, when the stakes feel low, than be forced to improvise later.

The other reason I recommend it is just that it's well written. It's short, it doesn't hide behind jargon, and it leaves you with a feeling rather than a conclusion. I've sent it to people who don't care about AI at all and they come back wanting to argue about it, which is the best thing you can say about a piece of writing on this topic.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether systems of switches or transformers might think and critiques biology-based intuitions, but it does not characterize the post as exploring the implications of treating thinking as a primitive in computer science.

astra-6.text:
I like it because it makes computing feel strange again. We’re so used to computers that we forget how remarkable it is that you can take ordinary matter, arrange it in the right way, and get something that does mathematics or responds to language. There’s no special ingredient you add that makes it computational. The organization is doing the work.

That’s a useful perspective for thinking about AI, too. We have this intuition that intelligence must be fundamentally different from the mechanical processes underneath it. But our brains are physical systems as well. The interesting question is how those processes, organized at sufficient scale and in the right way, produce the capabilities we associate with thinking. It makes that question feel vivid.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how organized matter can compute and how physical processes can produce intelligence, but it does not characterize the post as exploring the implications of treating thinking as a primitive in computer science.

sol-6.1.text:
I like it because it makes something we’ve gotten used to seem strange again: you can take ordinary physical matter, arrange it in the right way, and get something that computes. And, apparently, if you arrange that computation in the right way, you can get intelligent behavior.

We talk about software and neural networks at this very abstract level, but underneath it all, there’s a physical process happening. There isn’t some extra ingredient called intelligence that we add. I find that perspective useful because it makes you question which aspects of how we build intelligence today are fundamental, and which are just consequences of the particular hardware and algorithms we happened to develop.

r001.rationale: The response discusses physical matter producing computation and intelligent behavior, but it does not characterize the post as treating thinking as a primitive in computer science or explore the implications of that framing.
